disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of difficulties with sustaining attention, organization, and follow-through that cause impairment across settings, without prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Symptoms typically begin in childhood, though functional impact may become more evident later when environmental demands increase, such as in higher-level schooling or complex work roles. The course is usually chronic, with some individuals developing compensatory strategies that can partially mask deficits until life stressors or cognitive load exceed their coping capacity. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and cognitive disorders by its early onset, trait-like inattention across contexts, and lack of primary memory loss or fluctuating consciousness.

narrative.personality: Kristen is a sociable, detail-focused organizer who takes pride in keeping people and plans running smoothly while immersing herself in creative and community-oriented hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a few months ago, Kristen’s company completed a major digital transformation, adding multiple new software platforms, complex automated workflows, and hybrid meeting schedules for her to coordinate. For decades she had managed busy offices by relying on handwritten lists, over-checking her calendar, and staying late to make sure nothing slipped, but the rapid layering of digital tools and competing priorities pushed the complexity of her role beyond what those strategies could contain. As she tried to juggle mentoring junior staff, supporting several executives at once, and planning frequent events, she found that the sheer volume of small moving parts in her day-to-day work began to overwhelm her usual systems, spilling over into her volunteer commitments and elaborate social planning at home. When misplacements of paperwork, devices, and reference materials started to cause visible disruptions at work events and undermined her reputation as the “organized one,” she became distressed enough to consult a psychiatrist at the urging of a younger colleague who noticed how much she was struggling to keep track of essential items.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep misplacing important things I need for work and events, even when I think I’ve put them in the right place.”

narrative.personality: Marshall is a quiet, observant loner who channels his meticulous eye into security work and art, preferring structured routines and solitary, detail-oriented hobbies.
narrative.stressor: Roughly a year before seeking help, Marshall’s casino shifted from a traditional surveillance model to a fast-paced, AI-assisted system that required him to monitor multiple complex interfaces, document incidents in new software, and train younger guards while rotating between day and night shifts. He had always relied on a steady, methodical style—focusing on a few camera feeds at a time and keeping handwritten notes—but the new expectations for rapid multitasking, digital documentation, and mentoring disrupted his stable routines. As the technological demands and irregular hours increased, he noticed that the higher cognitive load and fragmented schedule made it harder for him to maintain the level of precision he prided himself on in both his security reviews and his model train and photography projects at home. When a series of small but significant oversights in his reports and video reviews led to criticism from supervisors and a formal performance review, he became worried about his job security and sought psychiatric evaluation to understand why he was suddenly making avoidable detail mistakes despite trying harder than ever.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep missing small but important details at work, and it’s starting to show up as mistakes in my reports and video reviews.”

narrative.personality: Christopher is a socially outgoing, competitively driven young man who enjoys challenges and improvising solutions but tends to be casual about planning and structure.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a month ago, Christopher was moved from a more routine filing role into a position that required frequent data entry, cross-checking documents, and managing several small projects at once for multiple supervisors. He initially welcomed the challenge and relied on his energy and competitiveness to stay ahead of deadlines, but the increased volume of fine-grained paperwork, shifting priorities, and ad hoc requests made it harder for him to rely on memory and informal systems. As he tried to balance longer workdays with late-night gaming, social activities, and weekend volunteer events, the accumulation of small administrative tasks began to outstrip his loosely structured approach to planning. After being called out for repeated minor errors in spreadsheets and forms that affected coworkers’ work, and noticing similar lapses in everyday tasks like managing bills and errands, he decided to see a psychiatrist to figure out why he kept making simple mistakes despite feeling motivated and capable.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep making simple mistakes on forms and spreadsheets at work, even when I think I’ve double-checked them.”
